claims.text: Greg Short asserts that the most dangerous position for an entrepreneur is life at a 7 out of 10 — comfortable enough to pay bills and avoid obvious pain, but not bad enough to force a change. At a 7/10, the entrepreneur will not leave a toxic partner, a toxic job, or a toxic business because the discomfort of the status quo is below the threshold that triggers action.
claims.speaker: Greg Short
conditions: Applies to entrepreneurs (and people trying to better themselves) whose current situation is tolerable but suboptimal
The status quo must be above outright crisis (i.e., not a 1-2/10 forcing immediate change)
claims.mechanism: Sufficient comfort suppresses the pain signal that would otherwise force corrective action; without enough pain, the cost of change appears to exceed the cost of staying, so no change occurs.

anchors.value: Pain is acute enough to force change
Comfortable enough to pay bills; not bad enough to leave toxic situation
The bigger opportunity Greg Short chose to pursue by abandoning 7-8/10 businesses

bounded_by: Does not apply when the entrepreneur is already in acute crisis (too little comfort to sustain inaction)
Does not apply to people who have developed a deliberate practice of periodically reassessing whether good-enough is the enemy of great

claims.text: Greg Short asserts that high-performing entrepreneurs — whom he calls 'savages' — are distinguished by their willingness to walk away from an 8/10 situation to pursue a 10/10 opportunity, even when the 8/10 provides strong current income and status. He states he has personally done this a dozen times, abandoning 7 or 8 out of 10 businesses to pursue larger opportunities.
claims.speaker: Greg Short
conditions: Applies to entrepreneurs who have identified a materially larger opportunity (a 10/10) that requires abandoning a functioning good-enough business (7-8/10)
Applies when the larger opportunity cannot be pursued alongside the existing business — opportunity cost is real, not hypothetical
bounded_by: Greg Short does not address financial obligations (debts, payroll, investor commitments) that may prevent abandoning an existing business
He does not define objective criteria for identifying a true 10/10 opportunity vs. a shiny object

examples.text: Greg Short states he has personally abandoned 7 or 8 out of 10 businesses approximately a dozen times in order to pursue larger 10 out of 10 opportunities. He presents this as the lived pattern he has observed in every high-performing entrepreneur he has met — the willingness to leave a comfortable, paying situation behind rather than allow comfort to cap ambition.

practices.text: Periodically audit your current business or situation on a 1-10 satisfaction and potential scale; if you are sitting at a 7-8/10, actively ask whether a larger 10/10 opportunity exists that comfort is preventing you from pursuing.
